tier_reason: The wiki Speed-Comparison page (last edited 2023-03-01) has first-party times for Vibrato 0.5.0 and MeCab 2020-09-14 on an i9-12900K. The harness is public (legalforce-research/tokenizer-speed-bench, tag vibrato-0.5.0-benchmark: compile_all.sh, run_all.sh, bench/mecab-unidic-3_1_1-bench/main.cc, bench/vibrato-bench/src/main.rs) and its flags are visible, but neither the g++ nor the rustc version is stated anywhere. Under the project's precedent a missing compiler version keeps it out of A, and the authors' own run is not B, so it stays C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: From tokenizer-speed-bench compile_all.sh (tag vibrato-0.5.0-benchmark): MeCab (taku910/mecab submodule) is built with its own ./configure, whose configure.in sets CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS to '-O3 -Wall' under GCC. The MeCab driver is built with 'g++ -std=c++11 -O3 ./main.cc -lmecab'. The Vibrato 0.5.0 crate is built with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-feature=+avx2' cargo build --release (release profile, opt-level 3). No gcc or rustc version is stated, and MeCab gets no -march, so only the Rust side is built for AVX2.
corrections.workload: Tokenize all 2,346 lines (158.8 characters on average) of 'I Am a Cat' (Aozora Bunko). Each tool reads the lines into memory, then times only the tokenization loop with a steady clock, single-threaded. run_all.sh runs 101 iterations, each a fresh process, and iteration 0 is a warm-up. MeCab uses mecab-ipadic 2.7.0 or unidic-cwj 3.1.1, and Vibrato uses its v0.5.0 precompiled dictionaries built from the same sources. The MeCab driver calls tagger->parse() with -Owakati, which builds a space-separated output string. The Vibrato driver calls worker.tokenize() and only counts tokens.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark run by the authors' organisation (LegalForce / daac-tools): one corpus (one novel) on one machine. Compiler versions are not stated. The two sides do not do equal work. (1) MeCab's parse() with -Owakati formats an output string, while Vibrato only builds the lattice and counts tokens. (2) Vibrato runs with default settings, not the MeCab-compatible -S -M 24 options, so its tokens can differ from MeCab's (README 'MeCab-compatible options'), and outputs were not compared. (3) Only Vibrato is compiled with AVX2 (+avx2); MeCab uses generic x86-64 -O3. (4) MeCab mmaps its dictionary and 459 MiB unidic matrix, so the timed loop likely pays page faults that Vibrato, which reads the whole dictionary into memory before timing, does not. This is an inference from the harness, not a measurement. The raw-connector compact model (1364 ms) is 7.6x slower than MeCab, and the dual-connector model (170 ms) is roughly level with it. The speedup is largest with the large-matrix unidic dictionary. The numbers are for Vibrato 0.5.0 (early 2023) and have not been re-run for later releases.

notes: Numbers match the wiki exactly: ipadic 42 vs 87 ms (2.07x) and unidic 75 vs 179 ms (2.39x), derived from page data. The baseline is MeCab built at -O3 by its own configure, so the C++ side is not crippled. The gain is a reimplementation with a different data layout (cache-efficient id mapping of the connection matrix) plus a lighter timed path, not a Rust codegen effect. Shortcomings to record: no compiler versions, AVX2 only on the Vibrato side, MeCab formats -Owakati output while Vibrato only counts tokens, outputs not checked equal (non-compatible default mode), and likely mmap page faults inside MeCab's timed loop (inference).

tier_reason: The README Benchmark section gives first-party hyperfine results against GNU find (19.922 s, 11.226 s and 854.8 ms; '23 times' and '13 times'). The scripts are public (sharkdp/fd-benchmarks warm-cache-simple-pattern.sh, config.sh, prelude.sh). There is no CPU, no fd or find version, no build flags, and the dataset is the author's own home folder, so it is not reproducible: C. WebSearch found no independent suite.

corrections.workload: Search the author's home folder (about 750,000 subdirectories and about 4 million files) for names ending in [0-9].jpg with a warm disk cache, timed with hyperfine. The commands were find ~ -iregex '.*[0-9]\.jpg$', find ~ -iname '*[0-9].jpg' and fd -u '[0-9]\.jpg$' ~ (fd-benchmarks warm-cache-simple-pattern.sh uses fd -HI, 5 warm-up runs, and diffs the outputs). Both tools returned the same 546 files.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark on one unnamed machine against the author's own home directory. The README says 'one particular benchmark on one particular machine'. fd, find and compiler versions are not stated, and nor is GNU find's build (distribution packages are usually -O2). fd walks directories in parallel with one thread per core by default, while GNU find is single-threaded. The task is dominated by pattern matching: find -iregex uses gnulib regex on the full path, and -iname uses case-folding fnmatch. Without a pattern the gap disappears. In sharkdp/fd issue #304 (2018, fd 7.0-7.1, Linux source tree, warm cache, no hardware stated), multi-threaded fd -HI -t f only reached parity with 'find . -type f' (69.1 ms vs 68.9 ms after commit 50a2bab), and fd -j1 was 1.49x slower than find. In the reporter's home-directory runs find was 2.15x (warm) and 1.85x (cold) faster than fd 7.0.0. So the README's 13-23x is a parallelism plus regex-engine win on a filtering query, not a codegen win, and single-threaded fd is slower than find on plain traversal. The README credits the regex and ignore crates (shared with ripgrep).

notes: Numbers and the 546-file equality check match the README verbatim. Metadata is confirmed: MIT OR Apache-2.0, 44.8k stars, last commit 2026-10-06, not archived. Shortcomings to record: first-party, no hardware or versions, private dataset, a parallel versus single-threaded comparison, and issue #304 shows find matching or beating fd on unfiltered listing and fd -j1 1.49x slower than find.

tier_reason: BENCHMARKS.md in lightpanda-io/demo is the vendor's own benchmark against headless Chrome 143. The code is public (chromedp/crawler, puppeteer/cdp.js), and it gives the Lightpanda commit and the Chrome versions. The Lightpanda build mode is not stated and the CPU model appears only in a neofetch image. The company sells the product, so vendor evidence is C. WebSearch found no independent reproduction.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: '16x lighter and 9x faster than Chromium'. Its table is labelled '(100 pages)', but its numbers (123MB vs 2GB, 5s vs 46s) match the BENCHMARKS.md 25-way rows: Lightpanda 25 processes 4.81 s, 123.0M versus Chrome 25 tabs 46.70 s, 2.0G (about 9.7x faster, 16x less memory, derived from page data). Other rows from the same table: 1 process versus 1 tab, 51.68 s, 27.2M versus 1:22.83, 1.3G (1.6x faster, derived from page data). 100 processes versus 100 tabs, 5.23 s, 410.2M versus 1:09.37, 4.2G (about 13x, derived from page data). Best versus best is 4.81 s versus 45.62 s for Chrome at 10 tabs (about 9.5x, derived from page data). Campfire page, 100 local loads via Puppeteer: average 16 ms versus 185 ms (total 1,698 ms versus 18,551 ms, about 11x), peak memory 21.2M versus 402.1M, peak CPU 4.6% versus 158.6%.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Lightpanda commit 7b1f157cf8ccbdded7db6ab47e94577495ee87e4. The build mode is not stated; the README says Zig 0.15.2 and the Campfire section points to the nightly release binary. The baseline is the official Google Chrome binary, 143.0.7499.169 for the crawler and 143.0.7499.109 for Campfire, started with --headless=new --remote-debugging-port=9222 (crawler also --user-data-dir=/tmp/bench_chrome).
corrections.hardware: AWS m5.xlarge (x86_64), fresh Ubuntu install, per BENCHMARKS.md; the CPU model appears only in a neofetch screenshot that was not read. The README calls the same crawler benchmark an m5.large.
corrections.workload: Crawler: a Go chromedp program crawls the Amiibo demo site (933 URLs) over the live internet. Chrome runs 1-100 tabs in one browser, while Lightpanda runs 1-100 separate processes (--fork --lpd-path), because Lightpanda cannot open multiple tabs. Each configuration ran once with /usr/bin/time -v, and smem PSS and ps CPU were sampled every 100 ms (watch -n0.1) for peak memory. Campfire: a homemade fake e-commerce page that loads two JSON XHRs, served locally, loaded 100 times via Puppeteer over CDP.
corrections.caveats: Vendor benchmark (Lightpanda sells a cloud service), so first-party. The two browsers do unequal work: Lightpanda has 'No graphical rendering engine' (README), so it skips style, layout, paint, compositing and Chrome's GPU and renderer processes. The JavaScript runs on V8 (C++) in both browsers; Lightpanda also uses libcurl (C) for HTTP and html5ever (Rust) for HTML parsing. So the gap comes from doing less work, not from Zig codegen. The authors chose a homemade page because Lightpanda 'is not yet fully compliant'. The crawler fetches pages over the internet, so its single-process runs are network-bound (6-11% CPU). The concurrency models differ (N processes versus N tabs). There is one run per configuration with no variance. The README's '(100 pages)' label does not match the 25-way rows its numbers come from. The summary table has a typo (1:09:37 for 1:09.37). The instance size is m5.xlarge in BENCHMARKS.md but m5.large in the README. No independent reproduction was found; a Wavect write-up (WebSearch, snippet only) notes it was not reproduced. The category is a poor fit for a language-level claim.
corrections.why_faster: No language mechanism is given or apparent. The README attributes the speed to building from scratch with no graphical rendering engine, while JavaScript still runs in V8 (C++, the same engine as Chrome). The time and memory saved come from skipping rendering and the multi-process Chromium architecture.

notes: Numbers are accurate to BENCHMARKS.md. The README '9x/16x' pairs the 25-process Lightpanda run with the 25-tab Chrome run, while one-to-one it is only 1.6x faster (51.68 s vs 82.83 s). Shortcomings to record: vendor benchmark; unequal work (no rendering engine); JS on the same C++ V8 engine, so no Zig-versus-C++ effect; a network-bound single run; mismatched instance size and labels; Lightpanda not fully web-compliant. Metadata is confirmed: AGPL-3.0, 36.3k stars, last commit 2026-10-11. Out of scope for the wave's language-level framing, but kept per the keep-and-document rule; the orchestrator may want a category override.
